en: Cross One Bridge, Read Both Banks: Yellow River Iron Bridge and White Pagoda Hill
zh: 过一座桥，看两岸：黄河铁桥、白塔山与黄河边
ja: 橋を一つ渡り、両岸を見る：黄河鉄橋・白塔山と黄河沿い

p.src: At the south end of Zhongshan Bridge, move out of the pedestrian flow before raising a camera. Look north along the deck and find three things in order: five steel truss spans, White Pagoda Hill rising directly from the north bank, and the pagoda above the tree line. Bridge, hill, and pagoda form one route. The crossing leaves the Chengguan old-city side and ends at the park entrance. The four guides show the scale of the bridge and hill; what matters on site is the simple alignment. Backlight, light haze, or foliage may hide the pagoda on a particular day. The steel bridge and the hill slope are still enough to establish the north-bank direction.

caption.zh: 五孔钢桁架横过黄河，白塔山从北岸抬起。先认出桥、山和塔，再决定上山深度。
caption.ja: 五つの鋼トラス径間の先に白塔山が立ち上がる。橋、山、塔の順を確かめてから、どこまで上るかを決める。
caption.en: Five steel truss spans cross the Yellow River as White Pagoda Hill rises from the north bank. Identify bridge, hill, and pagoda before choosing the climb.

p.src: This diagram is not a navigation map. It records one workable sequence: cross once from the south bank, confirm the park entrance at the north end, then reach the lower terraces. From there, the bridge, river, and park axis are visible and turning back is a complete visit. Continue to the White Pagoda precinct only when energy, weather, visibility, and the time before sunset all support the climb. After descending, choose one direction and one short riverfront segment, ending where the next meal, metro connection, or hotel route begins. No walking time is printed because route openings, construction, and wet or icy steps can change the day.

caption.zh: 从南岸过一次桥，在北岸入口选择下层台地或完整登高；下山后最多再接一段黄河边。
caption.ja: 南岸から一度だけ橋を渡り、北岸入口で下段テラスか塔院までかを選ぶ。下山後の川沿いは一区間に絞る。
caption.en: Cross once from the south bank, choose the lower terraces or full climb at the north-bank entrance, then add no more than one riverfront segment.

p.src: As checked in August 2026, Zhongshan Bridge is a pedestrian crossing; vehicle traffic ended in 2013. Pedestrian-only does not mean empty at every hour. Check four things before leaving and again at the bridge: weather, temporary riverfront controls, passage across the deck, and the ascent routes currently open in White Pagoda Hill Park. Strong wind, harsh sun, slippery conditions after rain or snow, or a dense crowd can turn the full climb into a lower-terrace visit. Do not squeeze this walk between two transport commitments while carrying large luggage. Store the luggage first, or visit White Pagoda Hill when no departure is imminent. Agree that separated travelers will meet at the south or north end; do not stand abreast in the middle of the bridge.

p.src: If the General Iron Pillar is visible near the south bank, do not dismiss it as an ordinary monument. The Zhenyuan floating bridge moved to the site of today's central crossing in 1385. Boats were linked, decked with timber, and held to the banks by iron chains; the structure had to be dismantled before winter ice and rebuilt in spring. It carried people, animals, and carts, but it could not stay in the river year-round. The General Iron Pillar survives from that anchoring system. Seen beside the fixed steel bridge, it makes the labour behind the old crossing easier to grasp: the difficulty lay not only in the river's width but in managing water, ice, wear, removal, and reconstruction. If temporary works obscure the pillar, keep the comparison and continue rather than detouring to hunt for it.

p.src: Now look up at the steel. The five through-truss spans completed in 1909 created a permanent central crossing in Lanzhou. The five curved upper members that now give the silhouette its strongest rhythm belong to the 1954 reinforcement. Distinguish those dates so that you do not mistake the entire structure for an unchanged relic of 1909. The lower trusses, piers, deck, and upper curves show changes from different periods of use and repair. While crossing, choose one span and notice its riveted members, then look back towards the old city and forward towards White Pagoda Hill. There is no need to guess the date of every piece of steel. Two facts are enough: the fixed iron bridge opened in 1909, and the 1954 reinforcement changed the profile visible today.

p.src: After crossing into White Pagoda Hill Park, the pagoda is not beside the gate. It stands above successive terraces and roofs. Look for three visual layers: pale stone rails and platforms rising below, tightly joined grey-green roofs in the middle, and the seven-level, eight-sided white pagoda at the top. They help locate your progress when paths branch and trees interrupt the view. The pagoda precinct is compact, not a broad summit square. Near it, check which entrance is usable that day and keep stairs and gateways clear while taking photographs. The buildings in front of you do not all belong to one period. From the start of the climb, distinguish the modern park terraces from the older temple precinct.

caption.zh: 七级白塔立在紧凑塔院与层叠公园之上。到入口再选下层台地或完整登高，不把所有屋顶看成同一时代。
caption.ja: 七層の白塔が小さな境内と段状の公園の上に立つ。入口で下段までか白塔寺の境内までかを選び、すべての屋根を同時代とは見なさない。
caption.en: The seven-level pagoda rises above a compact precinct and terraced park. Choose the lower terraces or full climb at the entrance, and do not treat every roof as one historical layer.

p.src: Decide how high to go at the north-bank entrance rather than committing to the full climb while still at the hotel. The lower terraces are enough to understand the bridge, river, and park axis, and they form a complete turnaround. Lower does not mean level or step-free. Continuing to the pagoda precinct requires a route open that day, a suitable surface, enough energy, usable visibility, and sufficient daylight for the descent. Drink before climbing in heat and leave a larger return margin in cold or after rain or snow. Stop at the lower level if knees or ankles hurt, a heavy bag remains on your back, or the group is already tired. Do not force the ascent for a single panoramic photograph. The value of climbing White Pagoda Hill is seeing how the two banks fit together; reaching the pagoda precinct is optional.

p.src: Continuing above the lower terraces means passing first through a mid-twentieth-century city park and then into an older pagoda precinct. The local garden gazetteer does not establish when a temple was first founded on the hill. Ruins of a White Pagoda monastery existed before 1448; reconstruction took place between 1448 and 1452, followed by further Ming and Qing additions. By contrast, the orderly three-terrace architectural group seen from the bridge was built mainly in 1958-1959, and the whole park opened in 1960. The present view is not one ancient landscape preserved unchanged. An older precinct was incorporated into a modern park axis, creating the sequence of bridge, terraces, and pagoda seen today. Do not label every upturned roof “Yuan dynasty”; equally, do not collapse the sequence into a simple old-versus-new story.

p.src: Looking back from the pagoda precinct or lower terraces completes the walk: you have crossed from the old-city side and chosen a suitable height on the north bank. If time remains, take one short riverfront segment in one direction, then continue to a meal, the hotel, or the next stop. Do not backtrack to add a waterwheel site, a boat ride, and another hill. Check boat operations, riverside access, and events on the day. If the weather turns, legs are tired, or dinner has a fixed time, return across the bridge or leave from the north bank. Time for the return, food, and rest is more useful than checking off every Yellow River sight.
